iable paleomagnetic poles (PPs) of early and mid-Paleozoic rocks in this continental block is thus very important for better understanding the tectonic evolution of southern South America. A sequence of Silurian-Devonian marine sedi- mentary rocks with intercalated ferriferous horizons, the Sierra Grande Formation, is exposed in north- eastern Patagonia. A preliminary paleomagnetic sampling of these rocks was carried out several years ago by one of the authors (JFV). The paleomagnetic study was started but, for technical reasons, could not be finished on that occasion. This study was finished recently, with the help of new and repaired instru- ments, as well as implementation of an integral com- puting system for paleomagnetism developed by Oviedo (1989). The results of this work, the first mid- Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from Patagonia, are reported here. GEOLOGY The Sierra Grande Formation is exposed in north- eastern Patagonia near the town of Sierra Grande (41.6°S, 65.4°W; Fig. 1). The formation is a mid- Paleozoic sedimentary sequence that covers the Pre- cambrian-early Paleozoic metamorphic and plutonic rocks constituting the North Patagonian Massif (Caminos and Llambias, 1984). A complete review of previous work and a description of this formation can be found in Zanettini (1981). Zanettini (1981) divided the Sierra Grande For- mation into two members. The lower, San Carlos Member consists of more than 500 ineters of marine quarzites, fine sandstones, siltstones, and shales. A ferriferous horizon, the Rosales horizon, is inter- calated at about the middle of the sequence. This horizon, the thickness of which varies between 10 and 30 meters, is composed of oolitic hematite, but mag- netite has also been reported (Zanettini, 1981). The upper, Herrada Member, is composed of red to pink and brown coarse, medium, and fine sandstones and some siltstones, and is a minimum of 1000 meters thick. Another ferriferous horizon, the Alfaro hori- zon, is also intercalated near the bottom of the Herrada Member. This horizon is seldom thicker than 10 meters and is also composed mainly of oolitic hematite. The age of the Sierra Grande Formation has been determined accurately by studies of its fossils. According to Mancefiido and Damborenea (1984), the fossils found in the lower member (Iterrada) indicate a Wenlockian age. The age of the upper member (San Carlos) is not as well constrained. Although it has been assigned to the Early Devonian (Zanettini, 1981), Mancefiido and Damborenea have argued that the paleontologic record is too poor to accurately de- fine the age of the Herrada Member and that it could also be Late Silurian. The upper member, therefore is here conservatively considered as Late Silurian- Early Devonian. Accor

carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: hand samples were collected from rocks of The San Carlos Member (not counting those from the Rosales horizon). Three were taken at site A1 (SG-203 to -205); six at site A2 (SG-206 to -211}; nine (originally ten but one was lost) at site F1 (SG- 262 to -270); and five at site F2 (SG-272 to -276). All of the samples were fine sandstones and, except those from site F1, belong to stratigraphic levels younger than the Rosales horizon. Paleomagnetic data ob- tained from these samples are presented in Table 2. Figure 5 shows the typical magnetic behavior of samples from site F (F1 and F2}. The AF technique was not useful for destroying magnetization (Fig. 5A), whereas thermal demagnetization showed a uni- vectorial magnetization stable at high temperatures (630°C), probably carried by hematite. A sequence of Silurian-Devonian marine sedi- mentary rocks with intercalated ferriferous horizons, the Sierra Grande Formation, is exposed in north- eastern Patagonia. A complete review of previous work and a description of this formation can be found in Zanettini (1981). Zanettini (1981) divided the Sierra Grande For- mation into two members. The lower, San Carlos Member consists of more than 500 ineters of marine quarzites, fine sandstones, siltstones, and shales. A ferriferous horizon, the Rosales horizon, is inter- calated at about the middle of the sequence. This horizon, the thickness of which varies between 10 and 30 meters, is composed of oolitic hematite, but mag- netite has also been reported (Zanettini, 1981). Another ferriferous horizon, the Alfaro hori- zon, is also intercalated near the bottom of the Herrada Member. All three components include normal and reversed sites. These ages coincide with the known Laramide, Goat River, and East Kootenay orogenies. Evidently, the terrane housing the Purcell Anticlinorium: (1) has always been part of the North American craton with little or no translation; (2) was folded and metamorphosed in the East Kootenay orogeny prior to 1400 Ma; (3) was thermally overprinted in the Goat River orogeny; and (4) was thermally overprinted and then rotated"" 37°± 12° clockwise as Terrane I of the Cordillera impacted from the southwest against the craton during the mid-Mesozoic Laramide orogeny. INTRODUCTION The Middle Proterozoic Belt-Purcell Super­ group is exposed in southeastern British Columbia and in contiguous parts of Alberta, Montana, Idaho, and Washington (Figure 1). The Aldridge Forma­ tion in Canada and the equivalent Prichard Forma­ tion in the United States are stratigraphically near the base of the supergroup. The Moyie sills intrude the lower part of the Aldridge (Prichard) Formation. The study area is in the Purcell anticlinorium where paleomagnetic fold tests can indicate if a given remanence component was formed before or after folding. The object of the study was to determine if this Precambrian terrane was rotated or translated relative to the North American craton, as was found in Mesozoic rocks of Terrane I of the Cordillera to the immediate west (Symons and Litallien, 1984). HILLHOUSE U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California The rocks of the Resurrection Peninsula compose an ophiolite (57+1 Ma) within the vast accretionary prism of the Chugach-Prince William terrane. Palcomagnetic data from pillow basalt and sheeted dikes of the ophiolite yield a mean palcolatitude of 540_+7 ø, which implies 13_+9 ø of poleward displacement. The characteristic component of the remanence resides in a Ti-poor titanomagnetite with a blocking temperature close to 580øC. A positive fold test and the petrology of the magnetic minerals lead us to conclude that the characteristic reinanent magnetization (ChRM) in the sheeted dikes originated as a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). We hypothesize that the ChRM of the pillow basalt originated as a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired soon after formation of the rocks during hydrothermal metamorphism. Structural data indicate polyphase deformation with folding about vertical and horizontal axes. The palcomagnetic data pass a fold test only when we incorporate this interpretation in our structura

se two terranes and, though usually easily identified in the eastern Gulf of Alaska region [Winkler and Plafker, 1975, 1981; Winkler et al., 1981], in the western Gulf of Alaska region it is difficult to discern which of many faults compose the Contact fault system [Tysdal and Case, 1979; Nelson 'et al., 1985; Bol and Coe, 1987; Dumoulin, 1987, 1988; Gibbons, 1988; Bol and Gibbons, in press]. In the eastern gulf, Chugach terrane rocks are generally more deformed and metamorphosed than the Prince William terrane rocks. In the western gulf, complex lithologic and structural relationships, a paucity of age control, and no distinctive petrographic breaks combine to obscure the terrane boundary. Due to this ambiguity in terrane distinction in the western gulf, we herein treat the two terranes as one: the Chugach-Prince William terrane. Palcomagnetic data from pillow basalt and sheeted dikes of the ophiolite yield a mean palcolatitude of 540_+7 ø, which implies 13_+9 ø of poleward displacement. The characteristic component of the remanence resides in a Ti-poor titanomagnetite with a blocking temperature close to 580øC. A positive fold test and the petrology of the magnetic minerals lead us to conclude that the characteristic reinanent magnetization (ChRM) in the sheeted dikes originated as a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). We hypothesize that the ChRM of the pillow basalt originated as a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired soon after formation of the rocks during hydrothermal metamorphism. In the eastern gulf, Chugach terrane rocks are generally more deformed and metamorphosed than the Prince William terrane rocks. In the western gulf, complex lithologic and structural relationships, a paucity of age control, and no distinctive petrographic breaks combine to obscure the terrane boundary. Due to this ambiguity in terrane distinction in the western gulf, we herein treat the two terranes as one: the Chugach-Prince William terrane. We envision a history where extrusion and quenching of pillow basalt with typical titanomagnetite (x = 0.6) was followed by low-temperature oxidation to produce titanomaghemite. Subsequent phase splitting to ilmenite + Ti-poor magnetite during hydrothermal metamorphism led to a CRM residing in the magnetite. Counterclockwise rotations of 50 ø to 80 ø are documented near the localities of Chala (eight sites), Ocon (two sites) and Arequipa (four sites). Preliminary results based on three sites of Late Permian to Early Triassic sediments from northern Bolivia also show a large counterclockwise rotation. The observed differences between the primary and the secondary magnetization indicate that large block rotations occurred prior to the acquisition of the secondary magnetization. Perhaps, this first episode of deformation partially structured the Andean chain in the Central Andes and induced an incipient orocline. During the Cenozoic, a differential shortening along the chain gave the present-day shape of the Bolivian deflection and resulted in a counterclockwise rotation of the forearc system by about 20 ø as indicated by the remagnetization. INTRODUCTION The Andes are considered a typical example of a mountain belt related to the subduction of an oceanic lithosphere beneath a continental plate [Dewey and Bird, 1970]. While subduction has been a continuous process since at least the Early Cretaceous, compressional deformations appear to have occurr

The Mesozoic volcanics from the coastal range outcrop mostly along the coast. The paleomagnetic sampling in Peru was made at several distinct localities referred hereafter in the text and figures as Chala, Ocofia, Arequipa, I1o, and La Yarada (Figure 1). Three sites in Late Permian and Early Triassic sediments [Martinez, 1980] from the Tiquina formation were also sampled near the lake Titicaca in Bolivia. Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. The Point Camden Gabbro The Hound Island Volcanics were intruded by 23-Ma gabbroic intrusions in the Keku Strait. We will informally refer to this unit as the Point Camden gabbro because of outcrop exposures at Point Camden on Kuiu Island (Figure 2). We have studied the paleomagnetism of these intrusions [Haeussler et al. this issue]; however, we evaluate the effects of these intrusions on the paleomagnetism of the Hound Island Volcanics in this paper. Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. The Point Camden Gabbro The Hound Island Volcanics were intruded by 23-Ma gabbroic intrusions in the Keku Strait. We will informally refer to this unit as the Point Camden gabbro because of outcrop exposures at Point Camden on Kuiu Island (Figure 2). We have studied the paleomagnetism of these intrusions [Haeussler et al. this issue]; however, we evaluate the effects of these intrusions on the paleomagnetism of the Hound Island Volcanics in this paper. Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. Because the Point Camden gabbro is more mafic than most rocks in the Kuiu-Etolin belt, and for the greatest tectonic significance of our paleomagnetic results we decided to obtain an isotopic age for the gabbro. An accurate date would also allow us to to constrain the thermal history and the age of overprints we found in the Hound Island Volcanics [see Haeussler et al., this issue]. To determine whether any such excess 40At is discernable in the plateau steps, the data were plotted on a 36Ar/4øAr versus 39Ar/40Ar isotope correlation diagram. Ten of the 13 \"plateau\" steps define an array that yields an isochron intercept date of 21.9 + 1.3 Ma (lc) with an initial 40Ar/36Ar intercept of 300.3 + 6.3, mean squared weighted deviation (MSWD) = 0.88. The initial 4øAr/36Ar isotopic composition is not signifi- cantly different from that of air (295.5), and (consequently) the isochron intercept date is indistinguishable from the plateau date. The 23.1 + 1.7 Ma \"plateau\" date is a reasonable estimate of the age of intrusion at site 76 because of the rapid cooling rate inferred for the gabbro (discussed below). COE Earth Sciences Board and Institute of Tectonics, University of California, Santa Cruz PAUL RENNE Department of Geology and Geophysics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey Samples of Tertiary gabbro from 24 sites in the Keku Strait, Alaska, help constrain the displacement history of the Alexander terrane. Step heating experiments on a plagioclase separate from these previously 40 39 undated intrusions indicate a discordant Ar/ Ar age of 23.1 + 1.7 Ma. The characteristic magnetization resides in magnetite, is easily isolated by thermal and alternating field demagnetization, and has both normal and reversed polarities. The mean paleomagnetic pole, with no stmctural correction, is latitude 87.1 øN, longi- tude 141.6øE, A95 = 10.1% with N = 20 sites. This pole indicates insignificant tectonic displacement (0.5 ø 4- 8.2 ø southward) and rotation (0.6 ø 4- 15.2 ø counterclockwise). The range in laboratory unblocking temperatures within a site is commonly small (often <40ø-50øC). If the rocks cool through this temperature range in a few thousand years or less, then a single specimen or locality would not completely aver- age secular variation. For example, Dodson et al. [1978] found that samples from vertical cores through the Tatoosh intrusion, in the Washington Cascade Range, display a paleomagnetic record similar to present secular variation records, and record a polarity transition of the Earth's magnetic field. Dodson et al. [1978] contended that because such a record is present, cooling rates in the pluton were fast enough to go through the blocking temperature range of the samples in a short period of time. Simple conductive cooling models for the Tatoosh are pre- cluded, because thermal modeling indicates it would take 80,000 years for samples 500 m from the margin of the pluton to cool from 580øC to 560øC; thus cooling by fluids seems to be called upon. Geological setting The Hercynian fold belt in northwestern Spain exhibits a zonation from high-grade metamorphic areas in the west to a non-metamorphic zone in the east (Julivert and Martinez, 1987). The As- turian arc is a thin-skinned fold-thrust belt, which is concave towards the foreland and whose s

of the thrust sheets and the irregularities produced by hanging-wall ramp anticlines, duplexes and an- tiformal stacks, made motion difficult. The exist- ing folds were tightened and the thrust sheets began to fold. The newly generated folds were essentially nucleated in pre-existing structures and were, therefore, longitudinal with respect to the older folds and thrusts. The radial folds super- posed on the above structures are best defined in the core of the Asturian arc and vanish towards its outer peripheries. Paleomagnetic data from Umbria (Italy): implications for the rotation of Adria and Mesozoic apparent polar wander paths. Tectonophysics, 216: 365-378. Sixteen new Jurassic and Cretaceous paleomagnetic sampling sites are located in northern Umbria along three river valleys (Basso, Burano, Sentino). The Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous data are consistent in declination, but not inclination, with previously published data from these valleys. Early Jurassic data from eight sites give site mean declinations which are significantly different from the two site mean declinations of this age which were previously available. Comparison of the data with Cretaceous and Jurassic mean directions from the Southern Alps indicate 20” anticlockwise rotation, relative to the Southern Alps, of this part of northern Umbria during Neogene deformation of the Umbrian fold and thrust belt. Introduction The Umbrian (or Umbrian-Marches) Apen- nines are an east- and northeast-vergent arcuate- shaped fold and thrust belt in central Italy (Lavecchia et al., 1988). In northern Umbria (Fig. 11, three rivers cut through NW-SE-oriented an- ticlines, providing excellent exposure of Umbrian Jurassic and Cretaceous stratigraphy. These are classic sections in southern Tethyan Mesozoic stratigraphy, with Rhaetian-Hettanginian shal- low-water Calcare Massiccio limestones suc- ceeded by Sinemurian-Eocene pelagic and seamount facies calcareous and siliceous sedi- ments, recording the Early Jurassic foundering of the carbonate platform and subsequent basinal development (Bortolotti et al., 1970; Bernoulli Correspondence to: J.E.T. Channel], Department of Geology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA. and Jenkyns, 1974; Cresta et al., 1989). The prin- cipal biostratigraphic control in the basinal sedi- ments is from foraminifera in the Upper Creta- ceous Scaglia, calcareous nannofossils in the Lower Cretaceous Maiolica, ammonites in the Toarcian-Aalenian Ammonitico Rosso and cal- care

ndenBerg et al. (1978). Apart from this important study, the vast majority of the available magnetostratigraphic and paleo- magnetic data in Umbria are from Cretaceous rocks, with few Jurassic data. In order to compare the pattern of Umbrian paleomagnetic directions with the African pattern, it is necessary to supple- ment existing Jurassic data. The deformation-related variation in paleo- magnetic declination in the Umbrian Apennines requires that we restrict our sampling to individ- ual sections which expose the Jurassic-Creta- ceous stratigraphy, in order to minimize the like- TABLE I 367 lihood of tectonic rotation between sites. We chose three NE-SW-oriented river valleys, sepa- rated by up to 20 km, which cut the Umbrian Apennines in northern Umbria (Fig. 1). ker and Clayton (1976). Occurrence of hematite Hematite occurs throughout the basin, most commonly in the basal part of the Manitou Falls Formation (Fig. 1). It imparts a dark purple to reddish color to the sandstones. In the Key Lake area, fine-grained hematite and specular hematite occur intergrown with early quartz overgrowths, as interstitial minerals in dark purple sandstones, and in reddish illite-rich alteration haloes surrounding uranium ore (Fig. 2). Thus, it appears that A, B, and possibly also C magnetizations are present across the entire basin. The drill-core data of Fahrig et al. (1978) also indicate that within a single drill hole, zones of A, B, and occasionally C magnetizations occur. Because their results contained both positive and negative inclinations, Fahrig et al. (1978) interpreted them as evidence for geomagnetic reversals during initial deposition of the sedi- ments. However, the hematite within the Athabasca Basin is diagenetic and possesses a CRM that was formed long after sedimentation. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. C., Canada V8L 3x9 Received November 5th, 199 1 Revision accepted April 9th, 1992 The Queen Charlotte Islands form the western margin of the Tertiary Queen Charlotte Basin, which is situated on the western margin of the North American Plate. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. Dykes, believed to be comagmatic with the plutons and volcanic rocks, are widely distributed throughout the islands, especially in the south. FIG. 4. They range in composition from basalt through andesite and dacite to rhyolite. All were formerly included in the Masset Formation (Sutherland Brown 1968), but Hickson (1988) now has suggested that the name Masset Formation be restricted to volcanic rocks of Late Oligocene to Late Miocene age (ca. 30 to 15 Ma). Using this relation- ship, Souther and Jessop (1991) suggested that the Kano plutons occupy the sites of magma columns and that the mean direc- tion of the associated dyke swarms is normal to the direction of least compressive stress during emplacement. Radiometric dates indicate that the predominantly north-trending dykes of the Collison Bay swarm were emplaced during the Middle to Late Eocene, whereas dykes of the east-trending Selwyn Inlet swarm were emplaced during the Middle Miocene (Table 1). It appears, therefore, that east -west extension was followed by north - south extension. They vary from less than 1 to 20 m in thickness, and composite dykes may be as much as 100 m across. Cumulative thickness of dykes is commonly less than 10% of the entire swarm width, but locally

Alteration is greatest close to subvol- canic plutons, where postintrusion hydrothermal activity has affected both dykes and their wall rocks. Opaque minerals commonly form less than 5 % of dyke rocks. Both oxide and sulfide phases are present as disseminated grains that rarely exceed 0.5 mm in longest dimension. Study of polished sections shows that a wide range of grain sizes, compositions, textures, and oxidation states is present. Titano- magnetite and ilmenite occur both as early-formed euhedral crystals and as anhedral grains occupying irregular voids between silicate minerals. Others now contain exsolu- tion of ilmenite in a magnetite matrix resulting in a very fine, patchy, moss-like or cross-hatched pattern having faint pleo- chroism. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. C., Canada V8L 3x9 Received November 5th, 199 1 Revision accepted April 9th, 1992 The Queen Charlotte Islands form the western margin of the Tertiary Queen Charlotte Basin, which is situated on the western margin of the North American Plate. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. PALEOMAGNETISM OF LOWER CRETACEOUS ROCKS 541 In the present study we have continued to search for rotations and displacements associated with the LOFZ. Initially we planned to sample rocks of early Cretaceous age thought to be pre- sent on both sides of the fault zone. However, as the study progressed it became clear that the age of the "early Cretaceous" rocks west of the LOFZ is very poorly constrained, and that the rocks themselves tend to be poor recorders of the an- cient geomagnetic field. Therefore, in this paper we shall present only results from east of the fault. 2. Regional geological setting In contrast to the central Andes, where episodic eastward migration of the magmatic arc and a well-developed forearc fold and thrust belt are present, the Andean Cordillera between 41°S and 49°S shows a uni

r trench-parallel strike-slip faults [20-22]. We speculate that the LOFZ has accommodated shear arising from oblique subduction of the Nazca plate, and also has partly controlled the location of the Cenozoic magmatic arc. In the region between 42°S and 44°S three distinct lithologic belts parallel the LOFZ (Fig. 1). These are, from west to east, the Coastal Range Paleozoic forearc accretionary complex [23,24], the North Patagonian batholith, and a sequence of Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous vol- canic and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks. The accretionary complex consists of low-grade metasedimentary rocks and interbedded tholeitic basalts. In the east these are intruded by the North Patagonian batholith (NPB), giving rise to isolated exposures of medium to high-grade metamorphic rocks. The NPB is composed of several distinct belts that grade eastward from mostly Mio-Pliocene granodiorites and tonalites to Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous monzogranites [16]. The western margin of the NPB is cut by the main trace of the LOFZ, along which younger intrusive bodies have been emplaced syntectoni- cally. PALEOMAGNETISM OF LOWER CRETACEOUS ROCKS 541 In the present study we have continued to search for rotations and displacements associated with the LOFZ. Initially we planned to sample rocks of early Cretaceous age thought to be pre- sent on both sides of the fault zone. However, as the study progressed it became clear that the age of the "early Cretaceous" rocks west of the LOFZ is very poorly constrained, and that the rocks themselves tend to be poor recorders of the an- cient geomagnetic field. Therefore, in this paper we shall present only results from east of the fault. 2. Regional geological setting In contrast to the central Andes, where episodic eastward migration of the magmatic arc and a well-developed forearc fold and thrust belt are present, the Andean Cordillera between 41°S and 49°S shows a uni

r trench-parallel strike-slip faults [20-22]. We speculate that the LOFZ has accommodated shear arising from oblique subduction of the Nazca plate, and also has partly controlled the location of the Cenozoic magmatic arc. In the region between 42°S and 44°S three distinct lithologic belts parallel the LOFZ (Fig. 1). These are, from west to east, the Coastal Range Paleozoic forearc accretionary complex [23,24], the North Patagonian batholith, and a sequence of Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous vol- canic and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks. The accretionary complex consists of low-grade metasedimentary rocks and interbedded tholeitic basalts. In the east these are intruded by the North Patagonian batholith (NPB), giving rise to isolated exposures of medium to high-grade metamorphic rocks. The NPB is composed of several distinct belts that grade eastward from mostly Mio-Pliocene granodiorites and tonalites to Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous monzogranites [16]. The western margin of the NPB is cut by the main trace of the LOFZ, along which younger intrusive bodies have been emplaced syntectoni- cally. Geological setting and sampling The Thvera subchronozonc in the Gilbert Chronozone was identified by a detailed magne- tostratigraphic study of the Eraclea Minoa sec- tion in the Caltanisetta basin of Southern Sicily (Fig. 1) [11]. The Eraclea Minoa section forms the basal part of the Rosscllo composite section [12] and it consists of marine marls of the Pliocene Trubi Formation (Fig. 2); the bedding plane at the sampling locality has a strike and a dip of 267°W and 14°N. The average sedimentation rate can be accurately determined on the basis of the astronomically calibrated polarity time scale (APTS) [13] and is 5.0 cm/kyr in the lower Thvera section and 4.4 cm/kyr in the upper Thvera section. The marls of the Trubi formation mainly consist of carbonates (60-80% CaCO 3) and a mixture of clay minerals [14]. Hilgen [15] recog- nized a long succession of small-scale sedimen- tary cycles--the so-called quadruplets. The weathering profile of these quadruplets form a repetition of grey, white, beige and white coloured beds (Fig. 2), which were deposited during cyclic sedimentation periods of approximately 19-23 ka. These sedimentary cycles are clearly related to the precessional cycle of the Earth's orbit [16].

These sedimentary cycles are clearly related to the precessional cycle of the Earth's orbit [16]. Although the weathering profile shows quite sharp changes in colour and induration, the changes in fresh, unweathered sediment are much more gradual. Considerable effort was taken to remove the weathered surface (up to 1 m) in order to expose the fresh (dark grey, light and dark blue) sediment. This method proved suc- cessful for almost the entire intervals sampled, except for the top part of the upper Thvcra interval where the uppermost white layer re- mained visibly and strongly weathered. In the lower Thvera interval the colour layering was not as clear as in the higher part of the section. Only a greyish and a beige layer could be distin- guished, while between these two layers there was a somewhat lighter coloured (white?) layer. Sampling was carried out by taking oriented cores, 25 mm in diameter, more or less parallel to the bedding plane at very close intervals (~ 1 cm), from a freshly cut, near-vertical plane. Introduction During most of the Cenozoic, South America drifted as an isolated continent carrying a unique biota. This isolation and faunal endemism changed after the formation of the Isthmus of Panama and the corresponding influx of immi- grant taxa from North America during the late Cenozoic, resulting in what has been termed the "Great American Interchange" [1,2]. This inter- change occurred in several phases, beginning in the late Miocene, about 8-9 myr ago, but the major phase of mammalian dispersal occurred during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, during the Uquian, Ensenadan, and Lujanian land mammal ages. The basin deposits of the central Andes of Bolivia preserve a rich sequence of mammalian faunal evolution for much of the Cenozoic. Hav- ing been deposited in a tectonically active setting, these basins often contain long, continuous strati- graphic sections of the kind amenable to magne- tostratigraphic analyses. Over the past few years, we have studied and sampled the late Cenozoic sediments surrounding the village of Inchasi in eastern Bolivia. Our collections have revealed a relatively rare pre-interchange mammalian fauna. These discoveries, in conjunction with new mag- netostratigraphic data presented for the Inchasi beds, allow a better understanding of the en- demic mammals and precise calibration of the Pliocene of the central Andes. It is perhaps significant that results reported to be of Devonian age from two rock units in the USSR (Table 1) resemble Devonian results from Britain. They are, however, of limited reliability and should be interpreted with caution. It is timely that a re-evaluation of palaeomagnetic data from the Russian plate (including the Russian platform) be made, enabling proper comparison of Russian and British data. We have already intimated that this would leave a large Mid-Palaeozoic gap in the APW record for the Russian plate. It is perhaps significant that results reported to be of Devonian age from two rock units in the USSR (Table 1) resemble Devonian results from Britain. They are, however, of limited reliability and should be interpreted with caution. It is timely that a re-evaluation of palaeomagnetic data from the Russian plate (including the Russian platform) be made, enabling proper comparison of Russian and British data. We have already intimated that this would leave a large Mid-Palaeozoic gap in the APW record for the Russian plate. Therefore new field work and palaeomag- netic analysis have been carried out on Siluro-Devonian rocks of the Russian platform in an attempt to unveil demonstrably primary remanent magnetizations and so fill in the gap in APW. This paper offers a detailed description of those new data and of their implications for the timing of assembly of the ‘Old Red Continent’. Received 1991 August 1; in original form 1991 January 7 SUMMARY Palaeomagnetic results from mainly Cretaceous rocks in Honduras delineate a distinctive apparent polar wander path (APWP) which is well suited for mag- netostratigraphy. The APWP is based on palaeomagnetic data from palaeontologi- cally dated units in the established stratigraphic column and three radiometrically dated intrusions. The ages and stratigraphic positions of sedimentary units whose stratigraphic assignments have been debated, can be inferred by comparing their palaeomagnetic pole postion with the known APWP. The results demonstrate the usefulness of magnetostratigraphy for resolving stratigraphic problems in the absence of fossils or marker beds, and for areas of discontinuous exposures. For regional interpretations, the most important conclusion is that strata in Honduras that have been assigned to the Todos Santos Formation were not deposited on the same tectonic plate as the Todos Santos Formation of Guatemala and southern Mexico. There is no evidence that the Honduran ‘Todos Santos’ strata are depositionally related to the true Todos Santos Formation. The name ‘Todos Santos Formation’ should be abandoned in Honduras and for the enti

t lake sediments (e.g. Creer & Tucholka 1982) as well as older rocks (e.g. GrommC, McKee & Blake 1972). Another means of using palaeomagnetism for correlation is to compare the magnetic pole position of an unknown rock unit with the pole positions obtained from an established stratigraphic column. This will not only yield a relative age, but also an absolute age with an accuracy which depends on the age resolution of the known apparent polar wander path as well as the associated errors in the palaeomagnetic data (e.g. Porath 1967; Kyle, Ulrich & Gose 1987). Palaeomagnetic results from the Mesozoic section of Honduras delineate an apparent polar wander path which is well suited for this approach. Critical to our work is the fact that some of the rock units had been dated either by fossils or radiometrically. These dated units form the ‘calibration points’ for the apparent polar wander path, from which the ages and stratigraphic positions of unknown rock units can be inferred by comparison. Another means of using palaeomagnetism for correlation is to compare the magnetic pole position of an unknown rock unit with the pole positions obtained from an established stratigraphic column. This will not only yield a relative age, but also an absolute age with an accuracy which depends on the age resolution of the known apparent polar wander path as well as the associated errors in the palaeomagnetic data (e.g. Porath 1967; Kyle, Ulrich & Gose 1987). Palaeomagnetic results from the Mesozoic section of Honduras delineate an apparent polar wander path which is well suited for this approach. Critical to our work is the fact that some of the rock units had been dated either by fossils or radiometrically. These dated units form the ‘calibration points’ for the apparent polar wander path, from which the ages and stratigraphic positions of unknown rock units can be inferred by comparison. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: d petrologic studies fail, paleomagnetic methods may afford a useful tool with which to evaluate the amount of tilting or flexing [e.g., Beck, 1980; Faulds et al., 1988b; Dagley and Piper, 1989; Marquis and Irving, 1990]. Accurate determination of the magnitude of tilting (or flexing) of crystalline rocks with paleomagnetic data is contingent upon magnetic mineralogy and structural level of exposure. The survival of a well-defined pretilt characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) generally requires an assemblage of dominantly fine-grained (i.e., single and/or pseudo-single domain) low-Ti titanomagnetite of relatively high coercivity and moderate to high unblocking temperature, or hematite, the paragenesis of which can be determined. The presence of such magnetic grain assemblages does not guarantee, however, that a pretilt ChRM is preserved. The preservation of a pretilt ChRM is less likely at deeper crustal levels [Beck, 1980], as the probability of magnetization unblocking increases at elevated temperatures. A magnetization may even be unblocked below short-term unblocking temperatures if elevated temperatures are maintained for long periods of time [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. Consequently, the ChRM of crystalline rocks may commonly be a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization (VPTRM), acquired during uplift-induced cooling, rather than a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: d petrologic studies fail, paleomagnetic methods may afford a useful tool with which to evaluate the amount of tilting or flexing [e.g., Beck, 1980; Faulds et al., 1988b; Dagley and Piper, 1989; Marquis and Irving, 1990]. Accurate determination of the magnitude of tilting (or flexing) of crystalline rocks with paleomagnetic data is contingent upon magnetic mineralogy and structural level of exposure. The survival of a well-defined pretilt characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) generally requires an assemblage of dominantly fine-grained (i.e., single and/or pseudo-single domain) low-Ti titanomagnetite of relatively high coercivity and moderate to high unblocking temperature, or hematite, the paragenesis of which can be determined. The presence of such magnetic grain assemblages does not guarantee, however, that a pretilt ChRM is preserved. The preservation of a pretilt ChRM is less likely at deeper crustal levels [Beck, 1980], as the probability of magnetization unblocking increases at elevated temperatures. A magnetization may even be unblocked below short-term unblocking temperatures if elevated temperatures are maintained for long periods of time [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. Consequently, the ChRM of crystalline rocks may commonly be a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization (VPTRM), acquired during uplift-induced cooling, rather than a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). METHODS AND PROCEDURES Representative pilot samples (about 25% of the total) were sub- jected to detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization. METHODS AND PROCEDURES Representative pilot samples (about 25% of the total) were sub- jected to detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization. According to the results thus obtained, the optimal steps were chosen for the remaining part of the collection. Two speci- mens from a hand sample were always heated, their mutual orientation having been changed after each step. All measurements were made on a Czechoslovakian spin magnetometer (JR-4). The data were analyzed with stereonets and orthogonal diagrams. After isolation of components, mean vectors were calculated for each hand sample. These sample means, be- ing independent spot readings of the ancient geomagnetic field, were in turn used for computation of local- ity means or site means. The fold test, applied to each lo- cality separately, was performed in two ways: as a test (CP test) based on the ratio of in situ and tilt- corrected concentration parameters [McElhinny, 1964] and as another one (M test) based on comparison of mean vectors [McFadden and Jones, 1981]. Palaeomagnetic results from the late Precambrian Chela Group of southwest Angola. Precambrian Res., 59: l-l 3. Palaeomagnetic results from fourteen sites (56 samples) in the late Precambrian Chela Group of southwest Angola are reported. After alternating field demagnetization eight of the sites have mean directions closely grouped around D = 123 °, I=-44½°; the dispersion of these directions increases substantially after tectonic corrections suggesting magnetic overprinting. magnetic components. After removal of viscous components, samples from five sites (Group 1) show a single component, similar to that observed after alternating field demagnetization. At four more sites (Group If) this same component is present together with another higher-temperature component. The mean direction for the component observed at all nine sites is D= 119.7 °, 1= -45.9 ° with k=40.5. Tectonic corrections produced little change in mean direction but reduced k to 4.5; the data supports the magnetic overprint hypothesis. A high blocking temperature component was resolved by remagneti- zation circle analysis of three flat-lying sites (Group Ill ) and this component is similar to the higher-temperature compo- nent observed at site DG (Group ll) after tectonic correction has been made. The component observed in Group Ill samples (D= 311 °, 1=49 ° ), confirmed by some samples from Group II, is similar to that observed in the Nosib Group just to the south in Namibia. It is suggested that the mean Group Ill result gives the primary direction of the Chela Group, that the data support the correlation of the Nosib and Chela Groups and that the Chela rocks were overprinted magnetically during an event sub- sequent to their tilting. The Akiyoshi limestone group is also an accreted reef complex originated on oceanic basaltic seamounts (KANMERA and NISHI, 1983). The Akiyoshi limestone ranges in age from early Carboniferous to late Permian, determined from the stratigraphic study finding fusuline and other fossils (OTA, 1977), and its accre- tionary emplacement probably took place in the late Permian to early Triassic times (KANMERA and NISHI, 1983). No paleomagnetic investigations of the Akiyoshi limestone group have been carried out in the past. The aims of this paper are as follows: (1) to reveal whether remanent magnetization of the Akiyoshi limestone is primary or secondary, (2) if a primary component is present, to deduce where the limestone was deposited, and/ or (3) if a secondary component is present, to tentatively assess the timing and cause of remagnetization. 2. This mean direction is almost the same as the in situ directions of welded tuffs from four formations distributed around the Akiyoshi Plateau, which have been already reported by previous study. These welded tuffs have fission track ages between 85 and 94 Ma. The remagnetized direction is also rather similar to the well-known paleomagnetic direction for Southwest Japan before about 15 Ma. These correspon- dences suggest that the Akiyoshi limestone and the welded tuffs were remagnetized by some event after about 90 Ma and before 15 Ma. Results of thermal demagneti- zation and observation in thin sections of the limestone suggest that dominant magnetic particle is magnetite, and that the limestone may not have suffered high temperature(>500℃)alteration. MORINAGA et al. 1981; HATTORI, 1982; HIROOKA et al., 1983; SHIBUYA et al., 1983; SHIBUYA and SASAJIMA, 1986). Because the terranes in Japan have repeatedly suffered severe tectonic move- ments, rocks in the terranes must have been located under an environment where they probably tended to acquire secondary magnetization. Based on detailed progressive thermal demagnetization treatments, SHIBUYA and SASAJIMA (1986) reported that red cherts and red siliceous mudstones from the Inuyama area in the southern part of the Mino terrane contain very stable secondary components. Radiolarian age determination (YAO et al.,1980) suggests the middle Triassic to the middle Jurassic age for these rocks. The Mino terrane was emplaced through accretion during the Jurassic (TAIRA et al., 1981). Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. These components can be resolved by an integrated cleaning approach such as AF-followed-TH demagnetization . The Aulis Volcanics, though of limited distribution, seem to be representative rocks for understanding the magnetomineralogical consequences of low-temperature oxidation. These rocks also show that the process of alteration and its magnetic consequence vary in accordance with the micro-environmental conditions , which in turn are time-dependent (STORETVEDT,1973). 116 P. Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. These components can be resolved by an integrated cleaning approach such as AF-followed-TH demagnetization . The Aulis Volcanics, though of limited distribution, seem to be representative rocks for understanding the magnetomineralogical consequences of low-temperature oxidation. These rocks also show that the process of alteration and its magnetic consequence vary in accordance with the micro-environmental conditions , which in turn are time-dependent (STORETVEDT,1973). 116 P. Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. These components can be resolved by an integrated cleaning approach such as AF-followed-TH demagnetization . The Aulis Volcanics, though of limited distribution, seem to be representative rocks for understanding the magnetomineralogical consequences of low-temperature oxidation. These rocks also show that the process of alteration and its magnetic consequence vary in accordance with the micro-environmental conditions , which in turn are time-dependent (STORETVEDT,1973). 116 P. Unless the sediments contain a source of hydrogen sulfide, the iron hydroxides and oxide are likely to be oxidized to hematite, which takes a few million years. Metamorphism is the other factor in the production of magnetic minerals. When rocks bearing, Fe, Ti02 and S2 are heated, pyrrhotite or hematite can be formed (MIYASHIR0, 1965). The alternative production of pyrrhotite or hematite is controlled by the O2 and S2 fugacities (ITAYA et al., 1985). Pyrrhotite never coexists with hematite, whereas magnetite can coexist with hematite. Metamorphism can produce a sedimentary layer which bears either hematite or pyrrhotite. The two hypotheses were examined through microscopic observation. Micro- Remagnetization of Cambrian to Triassic Sedimentary Rocks133 scopic study indicates that hematite-bearing slate and quartzite contain much authigenic magnesian and ferric minerals. They are composed of chlorite, white mica, and biotite. Authigenic fine magnesian and ferric minerals are also observed in the pyrrhotite-bearing Tumudong limestone. These facts strongly indicate that the sedimentary layers in the Paegunsan Syncline were more or less metamorphosed. A mean paleomagnetic direction(D=3.5° I=64.4° α95=5.10) of the Chichibu Quartz Diorite, obtained from 21 samples, shows no significantly deflected declination. Further, HYODO and NIITSUMA (1986) referred mean paleomagnetic directions of the Chichibu Tertiary System to clockwise rotation of the Kanto Mountains at about 94°since the Early Miocene. They explained this rotation by the opening of the Japan Sea(45°,15 Ma;OTOFUJI et al.,1985)and by the collision of the Tanzawa Block(45°, after 6-7 Ma;NIITSUMA,1982). On the other hand, ITOH (1988) carried out a paleomagnetic study on Late Cretaceous and Miocene rocks in the eastern part of Southwest Japan, and concluded that the bending motion occurred between 15 and 12 Ma. Thus several timings have been considered for the cusp formation. The Kanto Mountains are on the east wing of the cusp, and the Chichibu Quartz Diorite intrudes into the central part of the Kanto Mountains (Fig. 2). The radiometric ages of this quartz diorite determined by UENO and SHIBATA (1986) all indicate the Late Miocene (6-8 Ma). We measured paleomagnetism of the Chichibu Quartz Diorite and concluded that the cusp in the zonal structure had been formed in the Late Miocene or earlier. 2. The mean declination was significantly deflected from that of the expected direction calculated from the 20 Ma Eurasian mean paleopole. The deflection, -28.1°±14.0°, is explained by a counter- clockwise rotation of the Tsushima Islands relative to Eurasia after the igneous activity around 15 Ma. Introduction Since 1980, extensive paleomagnetic investigations have been carried out focusing on the rotational movements of Japanese island arcs (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983, 1984, 1987; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; OTOFUJI et al., 1985a, 1985b, 1985c; HAYASHIDA, 1986). These studies have revealed that a differential rotation took place between Southwest Japan and Northeast Japan in the Miocene time as a result of seaward rafting of continental fragments. The proposed tectonic event includes the breakup of the continental crust and subsequent back-arc spreading of the Japan Sea. The paleomagnetic directions sh

e) of the rotation has been roughly estimated at somewhere between the Korean * present address: Department of Earth Sciences , College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, Kyoto University, Kyoto 606, Japan ** present address: Tokyo Branch , Kawasaki Geological Engineering Co. Ltd., Tokyo 143, Japan. 797 798 N. ISHIKAWA et al. Peninsula and Kyushu Island (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983). The Tsushima Islands are located halfway between the Korean Peninsula and Kyushu Island at the southern margin of the Japan Sea (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic directions of the Cenozoic rocks on the islands enable us to characterize the tectonic movements associated with the formation of the Japan Sea. Before now, paleo- magnetic directions were available only from the Middle Miocene granitic rocks on the islands. The characteristic magnetization directions of the granite show counter- clockwise (CCW) deflection from the geocentric axial dipole field (ITO et al., 1980). The CCW-deflected direction may suggest that the Tsushima Islands were not included in the tectonic regime of the Southwest Japan block. Fig. 1. The CCW rotations of these islands imply that the Tsushima Strait area did not belong to the Southwest Japan block in terms of clock-wise (CW) rotation at about 15 Ma, constraining the western margin of the CW-rotated block. Introduction The Japan Sea-Japanese island-arcs is one of back-arc basin-island-arc systems on the eastern margin of Eurasia. The ages and opening histories of back-arc basins have been ordinarily revealed by means of identifications of magnetic anomaly stripes in the basins (e.g., WEISSEL, 1981). Howe

rcs implies the initiation of the Japan Sea opening prior to the opening accompanied with the CW rotation of the Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma (KANO and YANAGISAWA, 1989). Hence, it is indispensable to clarify the drifting mode of Southwest Japan in more detail, especially the extent of the CW-rotated block and the preferable position of the rotation pivot, for the better understanding of the whole process of the opening of the Japan Sea. The Tsushima Strait area between the Korean Peninsula and Kyushu Island is regarded as a boundary region between the stable Asian continent and the CW-rotated Southwest Japan block during the formation of the Japan Sea (Fig, 1). Miocene tectonics in the area must have been controlled by a relative motion between the two blocks. To reveal Miocene tectonics in the area will give a clue for clarifying the drifting mode of Southwest Japan, especially estimating the western extent of the block and the position of the rotation pivot. Seismic reflection profiles in the Tsushima Strait area show the existence of similar deformation features in the sea area (KATSURA and NAGANO, 1976; SAKURAI and NAGANO, 1976; NAGANO et al., 1976); the sediments in the area are acoustically divided into five stratigraphic layers, and the lowest layer is correlated to the Taishu Group or Goto Group on the profiles. The deformation features are recognized in the lowest layer between the two archipelagoes. SHIMADA (1977) suggested that fold and fault systems of the Taishu Group was formed due to a horizontal compressive force in NW-SE direction. On the basis of the similarity of deformation features of the pre-middle Miocene sediments, it is suggested that the Tsushima Strait area was subjected to compressive deformation after the deposition of pre-middle Miocene sediments. Since Miocene igneous rocks unconformably overlie and/or intrude the deformation features of the sediments on the two archipelagoes, the FT ages of the igneous rocks determined in this study constrain the timing of the compressive deformation to be at sometime in the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma. Untilted directions of primary magnetic components from early to middle Miocene sedimentary rocks in the Goto Islands dominantly showed counter-clockwise (CCW) deflections to the expected direction of the geocentric axial dipole field, while paleomagnetic directions from Miocene igneous rocks and Quaternary basalts were concordant with the expected direction. Zircon FT ages determined on sixteen Miocene igneous rocks show good agreement at about 15 Ma. These results, in conjunction with previously-reported paleomagnetic data in the Tsushima Islands, suggest that the Goto Islands were rotated at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma and that the CCW of the Tsushima islands occurred after about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands imply that the Tsushima Strait area did not belong to the Southwest Japan block in terms of clock-wise (CW) rotation at about 15 Ma, constraining the western margin of the CW-rotated block. direction. Zircon FT ages determined on sixteen Miocene igneous rocks show good agreement at about 15 Ma. These results, in conjunction with previously-reported paleomagnetic data in the Tsushima Islands, suggest that the Goto Islands were rotated at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma and that the CCW of the Tsushima islands occurred after about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands imply that the Tsushima Strait area did not belong to the Southwest Japan block in terms of clock-wise (CW) rotation at about 15 Ma, constraining the western margin of the CW-rotated block. The FT ages confine the time of the compressive deformation of pre-middle Miocene sediments in the area to be at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands probably took place in response to the movement of the fault system in the area associated with the compressive regime, especially a sinistral motion of the Tsushima-Goto tectonic line. The early to middle Miocene compressive deformation in the area occurred almost coeval with the opening of the Japan Sea. The compressive tectonic regime implies the convergence of the western margin of the Southwest Japan block to the Korean Peninsula during the CW rotation of the block at about 15 Ma, which gives a

tectonics in the area must have been controlled by a relative motion between the two blocks. To reveal Miocene tectonics in the area will give a clue for clarifying the drifting mode of Southwest Japan, especially estimating the western extent of the block and the position of the rotation pivot. A previous paleomagnetic study on the Tsushima Islands in the area suggested that the islands were rotated counter-clockwise (CCW) by about 28‹ sometime after the middle Miocene igneous activity on the islands (ISHIKAWA et al., 1989), which implies a different tectonic regime in the Tsushima Strait area from that of Southwest Japan during the formation process of the Japan Sea. In order to reveal Miocene tectonics in the Tsushima Strait area, we carried out a paleomagnetic study on Neogene rocks in the Goto Islands, another archipelago in the area, and fission-track analysis of Miocene igneous rocks in the Goto and Tsushima Islands. 2.
