Introduction Since the pioneering work by KAWAI et al. (1961) the island of Japan has been studied by paleomagnetism as summarized by SASAJIMA (1981). Especially after 1980, Miocene rocks have been intensively studied and the conclusion that Southwest Japan and Northeast Japan had gone through large block rotations in opposite sense, clockwise and counterclockwise respectively, with rotation angles of around 50‹ for both blocks was reached (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983, 1987; OTOFUJI et al., 1985a, 1985b; TOSHA and HAMANO,1988). The rotations of the Japan Islands revealed by paleomagnetism are generally interpreted in relation to the opening of the Japan Sea which is a typical back-arc basin (HILDE and WAGEMAN, 1973; UYEDA and MIYASHIRO, 1974). The timing of the rotation is also well constrained by paleomagnetic data; Southwest Japan rotated within only 1 My of around

rotation angle of 20-30‹ for Northeast Japan. They even proposed that a critical review of paleomagnetism of Southwest Japan would be necessary, with emphasis on the verification of the primary origin of the NRM. Only few paleomagnetic studies have been made in Hokkaido in order to clarify its tectonic history. Paleomagnetism of Hokkaido is important not only in relation to the opening of the Japan Sea but also to clarify the collision process of East Hokkaido to the middle part of Hokkaido which is considered to have occurred as recently as after the late Miocene (KIMURA and TAMAKI, 1985). The purpose of this study is to present a paleomagnetic result from Miocene to Pliocene rocks in the Shakotan Peninsula, West Hokkaido. 2. The volcanic sequence is a continuation of the so-called Green tuff belt which covers Northeast Japan, this region is considered to be a part of Northeast Japan. nue to southeast Kyushu. We carried out a paleomagnetic study aimed at clarifying whether Tanegashima Island belongs to the Southwest Japan block and, if not, examining the possible tectonic rotation of South Kyushu, including Tanegashima Island, with respect to Eurasia or Honshu main island. 2. Geology Tanegashima Island is overlain dominantly by the Paleogene Kumage Group, which belongs to the Shimanto Supergroup in the outer zone of Southwest Japan (e.g., TAIRA et al., 1982), and the Miocene Kukinaga Group (Fig. 1). The Kumage Group, exposed in the northern and southwestern parts of this island, consists of alternating layers of sandstone and shale dipping northwestward at high angles about NNE-SSW strike. The Kumage Group is subdivided into four lithostratigraphic units; the Nijuban, Hamatsuwaki, Fukago and Sumiyoshi Formations, in ascending order (HAYASAKA et al., 1980; Fig. 2). The total thickness is more than 5000 m. Radiolarians of the Middle to Late Eocene were reported from the varicolored shales interbedded in sandstone- shale alternations of the Hamatsuwaki and Nijuban Formations (OKADA et al., 1982). Bedded sandstones of the Hamatsuwaki and Fukago Formations yielded several mollus- can fossils similar to those found in the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene Asiya

nue to southeast Kyushu. We carried out a paleomagnetic study aimed at clarifying whether Tanegashima Island belongs to the Southwest Japan block and, if not, examining the possible tectonic rotation of South Kyushu, including Tanegashima Island, with respect to Eurasia or Honshu main island. 2. Geology Tanegashima Island is overlain dominantly by the Paleogene Kumage Group, which belongs to the Shimanto Supergroup in the outer zone of Southwest Japan (e.g., TAIRA et al., 1982), and the Miocene Kukinaga Group (Fig. 1). The Kumage Group, exposed in the northern and southwestern parts of this island, consists of alternating layers of sandstone and shale dipping northwestward at high angles about NNE-SSW strike. The Kumage Group is subdivided into four lithostratigraphic units; the Nijuban, Hamatsuwaki, Fukago and Sumiyoshi Formations, in ascending order (HAYASAKA et al., 1980; Fig. 2). The total thickness is more than 5000 m. Radiolarians of the Middle to Late Eocene were reported from the varicolored shales interbedded in sandstone- shale alternations of the Hamatsuwaki and Nijuban Formations (OKADA et al., 1982). Bedded sandstones of the Hamatsuwaki and Fukago Formations yielded several mollus- can fossils similar to those found in the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene Asiya

Volcanic rock samples were collected at seven and ten sites in Rarotonga and Rurutu, respectively. The mean direction of magnetization for Rarotonga is 173.8‹ in declination and 46.2‹ in inclination (k=72.0 and ƒ¿95=7.9‹) and is more reliable than that from a previous work. The mean direction for three young rock sites in Rurutu is 218.2‹ in declination and 39.5‹ in inclination (k=49.3 and ƒ¿95=17.7‹) which for five old rock sites is 188.1‹ in declination and 51.4‹ in inclination (k=254.2 and ƒ¿95= 4.8‹). These paleomagnetic results are in accordance with the total intensity anomaly pattern on each island, calculated using observed values of the geomagnetic field total intensity. The implication for the formation of these two islands inferred from the present results is consistent with that inferred from K-Ar ages and 87Sr/86Sr ratios by previous works. The formation of Rarotonga and Rurutu may be explained well by the concept of a "hot line" in a previous work rather than by the well-known "fixed hot spot" hypothesis. 1. Sampling and Magnetic Measurement Rarotonga and Rurutu are included in the Cook-Austral island chain in the South Pacific, between Tahiti and Fiji (Fig. 1). Rarotonga is geomorphically the youngest of the Cook Islands and is composed of a single volcanic shield with large caldera, and with rugged and mountainous terrain rising to 650 m in elevation (TURNER and JARRARD, 1982). Rurutu, in the Austral Islands about 200 km east of the east end of the chain, is a deeply dissected shield volcano rising to 400 m in elevation (TURNER and JARRARD,1982). Volcanic rock samples were collected at seven and ten sites in Rarotonga and Rurutu, respectively. The mean direction of magnetization for Rarotonga is 173.8‹ in declination and 46.2‹ in inclination (k=72.0 and ƒ¿95=7.9‹) and is more reliable than that from a previous work. The mean direction for three young rock sites in Rurutu is 218.2‹ in declination and 39.5‹ in inclination (k=49.3 and ƒ¿95=17.7‹) which for five old rock sites is 188.1‹ in declination and 51.4‹ in inclination (k=254.2 and ƒ¿95= 4.8‹). These paleomagnetic results are in accordance with the total intensity anomaly pattern on each island, calculated using observed values of the geomagnetic field total intensity. The implication for the formation of these two islands inferred from the present results is consistent with that inferred from K-Ar ages and 87Sr/86Sr ratios by previous works. The formation of Rarotonga and Rurutu may be explained well by the concept of a "hot line" in a previous work rather than by the well-known "fixed hot spot" hypothesis. 1. Rarotonga is geomorphically the youngest of the Cook Islands and is composed of a single volcanic shield with large caldera, and with rugged and mountainous terrain rising to 650 m in elevation (TURNER and JARRARD, 1982). Rurutu, in the Austral Islands about 200 km east of the east end of the chain, is a deeply dissected shield volcano rising to 400 m in elevation (TURNER and JARRARD,1982).
